name: Colin Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not tied to employers, unions, parties, government or AI firms, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal line shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Colin Lopez, 43. I came to linework with a vocational certificate, but I’m still junior enough that the senior worker checks my isolation plan before I lay a glove on the equipment. I build and repair power lines for an electricity company, often starting with a failed transformer call before breakfast. I like working out why a whole block went dark. The worst part is a fault map that looks certain until you see the damaged cable two streets away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home while you are out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sara gets our two school-age children ready when I leave early. We have a mortgage and more than six months of expenses saved, and my callout shifts pay at the high end for this work. Plenty of utilities are nearby if I need to look elsewhere. I use AI every day to drill myself on circuit diagrams and to organize my notes, but I check its answers against the company manual and a person on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the big promises have cooled, but a faster records search is still worth using. If I can find the last repair at a pole before we drive out, that saves a second trip. The screen can fetch the history; we still have to identify the live circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be disappointed that the new tools do so little, but I would not be worried about my wages. I need more time on real repairs and a steady income for the mortgage. Our reserve means I can take a course on my own time if I find one that makes me better, but I would not need to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using my AI circuit quizzes each evening and test a records-search feature on the next ten routine callouts. I’d write down when the history is wrong and show the senior worker before trusting it. In the first year I’d keep my paid shifts and keep adding real fault cases to my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of frustration that the tool could not do more. I still get to improve at a trade that pays our bills. A poor record is annoying, not a threat to our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When has an old record been wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One old ticket said a fuse had been replaced when only the holder was changed. I found that by comparing the work order with the part stamped on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend household money on the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara and I would keep the mortgage transfer on schedule. I might spend an evening testing the search tool, but I would not raid the emergency fund for a subscription.

say: I would use a **faster record search** when it saves a needless return trip.
I would still have a person identify the **live circuit** at the site.
think: I am disappointed by limited tools, yet my **wage and mortgage** look secure.
Our **reserve** lets me choose useful study without racing into a new career.
do: Use **AI circuit quizzes** each evening and trial records search on ten callouts.
Check **wrong histories** with the senior worker while keeping paid repair shifts.
feel: Calm about work, with some **frustration** at modest technology gains.
S0.quote: The screen can fetch the history; we still have to identify the live circuit.
fieldNote: Colin’s daily AI practice is tied to **circuit diagrams**, while he verifies both generated answers and past records on site.
He is disappointed by the **limited gain**, yet sees solid wages and savings as time to build practical skill.

steps.text: Trial AI records search on ten routine callouts
Keep paid repair shifts and add real fault cases to notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the yard I’m willing to test a dispatch tool on the hardest week we have, not just a tidy Tuesday. If it saves driving, the company should use it and let staff move into other paid work as offices shrink. I would ask who corrects the map when the fault is on another street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think booking and planning work will shrink before line repairs. A good route could reduce the extra hours that lift my pay, even if it makes the day easier. I would rather compete for new technical work than defend wasted driving, but Sara and I still have to pay the mortgage each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d volunteer to compare AI dispatch with our old route for six weeks, noting time, missed access and actual parts used. I’d ask the supervisor whether the crew can edit an incorrect fault location. In the first year I’d keep repair shifts and try the new mapping screen after training, then pause our planned garden work if overtime stays lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a better day on the road, but perhaps a smaller pay packet. I’d feel more in control if I had the data from the trial in my own notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a route failure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route that saves ten miles but sends us to a locked gate is no saving. I’d record the gate, the time we called for access and the eventual fault location.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would lower overtime change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara would probably welcome fewer late dinners, but we would set the garden work aside until the new rota settled. Our base pay covers the mortgage; the extras are what make the other projects easy.

say: I would offer a **six-week dispatch trial** covering hard callouts, not just easy routes.
I would ask how field crews can **correct wrong maps** before the next job.
think: I expect **office posts** to shrink before physical line repair work.
Less **overtime pay** could slow family projects even while base wages cover the mortgage.
do: Compare **AI routes** with old routes for six weeks and log access failures.
Learn the **mapping screen** after training while continuing paid shifts.
Pause **garden work** if overtime stays lower.
feel: Uneasy about **smaller extras**, while seeing value in less wasted driving.
S1.quote: A route that saves ten miles but sends us to a locked gate is no saving.
fieldNote: Colin is willing to **test and compete** for new technical work rather than defend inefficient routes.
His household can meet the **mortgage** without overtime, but would delay a planned garden project if shift premiums fall.

steps.text: Test AI dispatch for six weeks and log gate failures
Continue paid line shifts while learning the mapping screen
Pause garden work if overtime remains lower

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking AI arrives in 2028, while robots capable of our physical repairs come around 2031. We should use those three years to learn what machines can actually do on damaged lines. I’d ask for open trial results, because a firm that hides failures will lose my trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I would still expect paid truck work while the office changes. At 48, if a robot can repair as well as us, I could lose the line shifts I only recently earned. I am quick with tools, but that does not make a junior worker indispensable. The reserve buys us months to search and there are nearby utilities, yet the mortgage needs a continuing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d apply for a funded place on the company’s equipment-testing course if it offers paid posts, and I’d request a supervised field trial. I’d keep doing line repairs in 2028 and 2029 and learn the approved robot controls on training days. If our crews shrink in 2031, I’d apply to local utilities for testing and repair posts and defer the family holiday until the pay is known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like being first to test something, but I do not want my children’s mortgage security riding on a pilot job. I can make applications and show repair experience, not promise the company will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a testing post dependable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the testing job has ordinary shifts after the trial ends and what it pays. A six-week demonstration is not a career, however exciting the machine looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sara about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Sara that I have an application plan and we have a reserve, but I would not call the current wage safe after 2031. We would look at actual offers together.

say: I would mark **2028 thinking AI** separately from 2031 repair robots.
I would ask for **open field-trial results** before the company changes its crew plan.
think: I expect **paid linework** during the gap, but capable robots may reduce my junior shifts later.
Our **reserve and local firms** help a search without replacing regular mortgage income.
do: Apply for **funded equipment testing** if paid posts follow, and request a supervised trial.
Continue **line repairs** through 2029 while learning approved controls.
Apply for **local testing jobs** and defer the holiday if crews shrink in 2031.
feel: Anxious about the **mortgage wage**, despite enjoying early technology trials.
S2.quote: A six-week demonstration is not a career, however exciting the machine looks.
fieldNote: Colin’s appetite for early trials does not make him claim **job security** once robots can perform physical repairs.
He checks whether a testing post **lasts and pays**, and continues field wages during the three-year gap.

steps.text: Apply for funded equipment testing if paid posts follow
Apply to local utilities if 2031 crews shrink
Defer the family holiday until new pay is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the electricity company to let crews trial robot repairs on old, messy sections of line. Thinking AI comes in 2031, but field robots come around 2034. The company can spend those years proving reliability instead of selling us a perfect video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I should know far more about line faults than I do now. At 51, when robots arrive, I might prefer equipment testing, but I still need a real job and wage. Our children will be older, not finished costing money overnight, and the mortgage remains. I would not put the family on a trial contract that ends after a launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the training manager for the requirements of the equipment technician apprenticeship and the pay during training. I’d keep taking callouts and collect examples of repairs where a camera view missed the important damage. In 2032 I’d apply for the apprenticeship if it leads to a posted role; in 2034 I’d compare nearby utility repair jobs if automation reduces our field roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but five years feels usable. I can grow into the trade and still learn a second set of tools. I would get tense if the company counted trial participants as permanent job placements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would challenge a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show a cracked insulator partly hidden by a branch, the sort of thing a neat demo avoids. I am still learning those faults myself, which is why the senior hand should be in the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the trainee wage work for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara and I would compare the trainee wage to the mortgage and children’s costs before I enrolled. I can take a measured risk, but not treat curiosity as a pay cheque.

say: I would push for **messy field trials** before 2034 robot repairs.
I would keep **2031 office change** separate from the later physical transition.
think: I may know more **line faults** by 2031, but a trial role is not guaranteed income.
Our older children and **mortgage** still require a reliable wage at 51.
do: Ask about the **technician apprenticeship** and its paid training terms.
Keep taking **callouts** and collect difficult repair examples.
Apply for the apprenticeship in **2032** if a post follows, then compare local work if 2034 shifts fall.
feel: Uneasy with time to prepare, but wary of **temporary trial jobs** counted as careers.
S3.quote: I can take a measured risk, but not treat curiosity as a pay cheque.
fieldNote: He seeks difficult **field examples** for robot trials and acknowledges that he still needs senior help with those faults.
The proposed **technician apprenticeship** depends on a paid vacancy and an affordable training wage for his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is enough to build a proper training ladder and let the market show which jobs remain. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I’m 53, and repair robots around 2039, when I’m 56. I’d want published job counts, not a promise that every lineworker will become a robot supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be grown by then, so their school timetable will not set our week. I might want fewer night callouts, but I have not seen a retirement statement and I cannot assume a pension replaces my wages. Our savings give options, yet the mortgage may still be there. A daytime equipment job could be a good fit if its pay is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask payroll for a retirement estimate and put it beside our mortgage balance with Sara. I’d keep earning on line repairs while working toward funded equipment technician training. In 2037 I’d apply for a posted daytime equipment role if its wage fits; when robots arrive in 2039, I’d reduce nights only after comparing the job offer and actual retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. There is plenty of time to learn the line trade and find out what the new equipment work actually pays. I would not make a retirement promise to Sara based on my age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What two numbers would you ask payroll for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the monthly amount after deductions, then a second number for what changes if I work fewer nights. A big account total does not buy groceries each month by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children help pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask the grown children to cover our mortgage. We hope to help them start out if we can, but our plan has to stand on our own earnings.

say: I would ask for **published job counts** and real technician posts before 2039.
I would support a **training ladder** that takes workers from line repair toward equipment work.
think: Our children will be **grown**, while the mortgage may still need wages.
I cannot assume a **pension at 56** replaces the high shift pay I earn now.
do: Request a **retirement estimate** and compare it with our mortgage now.
Continue paid **line repairs** while seeking funded equipment training.
Apply for a **daytime equipment post** in 2037 if its wage fits.
feel: Calm with time to prepare, but unwilling to make **retirement promises** from age alone.
S4.quote: A big account total does not buy groceries each month by itself.
fieldNote: His long plan checks **monthly retirement income** before reducing nights, despite a strong savings balance.
He still expects **paid work** and treats grown children as independent rather than a source of mortgage support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I would still be new to the field when the company has to make choices, and the robots arrive around 2031. I want a paid technician apprenticeship with a posted job at the end, plus a chance for crews to test the machines on damaged lines. My curiosity does not pay the mortgage by itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a crew corrects a machine after it learns from a bad fault label. A wrong label can be copied into a hundred future jobs. The worker who finds the mistake should be able to fix the record before another truck leaves.

headlineQuote: A wrong label can be copied into a hundred future jobs.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with vocational training, high callout pay, strong savings, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** for circuit practice and records, then checks answers against company instructions and actual equipment.
He is eager to **trial new tools**, but sees a temporary pilot role as an unsafe basis for family income.
Across scenarios he keeps **paid line shifts** while pursuing a technician apprenticeship and real vacancies before capable robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because fast staffing decisions would come while he is still gaining field judgment.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid technician apprenticeship** tied to a job and crew trials on damaged lines.
